title: Types of Construction Contracts: What Specialty Trade Contractors Need to Know Before Signing a Subcontract
summary: Understand the main types of construction contracts and what each means for a specialty trade contractor's risk, cash flow, and compliance.
body_markdown:
The contract type on a construction project determines how a specialty trade contractor gets paid, how much risk sits on their side of the table, and how tightly labor costs need to be tracked. Signing a subcontract without understanding the underlying contract structure is how contractors end up absorbing costs they never priced, chasing change orders that go nowhere, or discovering too late that their margin evaporated because the project overran its budget. Every subcontractor should know what type of contract governs the project and what that means for their scope, their payroll, and their bottom line.


## **Why Contract Type Matters for Specialty Trade Contractors**


The general contractor picks the project. The owner picks the contract type. And the subcontractor inherits the terms, often with less negotiating power and more financial exposure per dollar of revenue. Understanding how each contract type allocates cost risk, schedule risk, and payment timing is not legal theory. For a trade contractor running tight margins, it is the difference between a profitable job and one that quietly eats the quarter.


### **How Contract Type Affects Your Labor Costs**


Labor represents the largest cost category for most specialty contractors. The contract type determines whether you carry the risk of labor cost overruns, share that risk with the owner, or pass it through on a cost-plus basis. Getting this wrong, or failing to track labor accurately, can wipe out margins on an otherwise well-executed job. Contractors using ​[real-time job costing](https://www.buildtrayd.com/2026/solutions/job-costing/projects) can see labor spend against the contract value daily, which matters most on fixed-price work where overruns come out of your pocket.


## **The Main Construction Contract Types Explained**


Each contract type shifts risk and reward differently between the owner, the general contractor, and the subcontractor. Below are the types of contracts specialty contractors encounter most often, with the practical implications for each.


### **Lump Sum (fixed-price) Contracts**


A lump sum contract sets a fixed total price for the defined scope of work. The contractor agrees to complete the work for that amount regardless of actual costs incurred. If costs come in below the lump sum, the contractor keeps the difference. If costs exceed it, the contractor absorbs the loss.


For a specialty trade subcontractor, lump sum work means accurate estimating is everything. Prevailing wage rates, union fringe obligations, anticipated overtime, material costs, and equipment needs all have to be priced correctly before the bid goes in. Once the contract is signed, there is limited room to recover unexpected labor costs unless the scope changes and a change order is approved.


Lump sum contracts demand tight ​[field and labor tracking](https://www.buildtrayd.com/2026/products/field-labortracking/worker-app) because every unbilled hour erodes the margin. Contractors who discover overruns at month-end instead of day-end lose the chance to adjust crew size, overtime, or sequencing before the damage is done.


### **Cost-Plus Contracts**


A cost-plus contract reimburses the contractor for actual costs (labor, materials, equipment, subcontractors) plus a fee, which is either a fixed amount or a percentage of costs. The owner bears the cost risk, and the contractor is compensated for what the work actually requires.


For subcontractors, cost-plus work reduces the risk of eating labor overruns, but it introduces documentation requirements. Every hour, every material purchase, and every piece of equipment must be tracked, categorized, and reported accurately. Owners and GCs on cost-plus projects often audit subcontractor costs closely, so sloppy records can lead to disputed invoices and delayed payment.


Cost-plus contracts are common on projects where scope is difficult to define upfront, such as renovation, remediation, or fast-tracked work. A subcontractor's ability to produce clean, auditable records of labor and material costs, backed by ​[construction payroll](https://www.buildtrayd.com/2026/products/payroll-new/edit-payroll) data, directly affects how quickly they get paid.


### **Time and Materials (T&M) Contracts**


A time and materials contract pays the contractor based on hourly labor rates (often with a markup) plus the cost of materials at cost or with a markup. T&M contracts are similar to cost-plus but simpler in structure, often used for smaller or undefined scopes where a lump sum would be impractical.


For specialty contractors, T&M work requires accurate timekeeping and clear documentation of labor hours by classification. Disputes often arise when the GC or owner challenges whether the hours billed were reasonable for the work performed. Having field-verified time records from a ​[foreman app](https://www.buildtrayd.com/2026/products/field-labortracking/foreman-app) or daily shift report strengthens the contractor's position.


### **Guaranteed Maximum Price (GMP) Contracts**


A GMP contract sets a ceiling on the total project cost. The contractor is reimbursed for actual costs (like cost-plus) but cannot exceed the guaranteed maximum. If costs come in under the GMP, savings are typically shared between the owner and the contractor according to a pre-agreed formula. If costs exceed the GMP, the contractor absorbs the overrun.


Subcontractors on GMP projects face a hybrid risk profile. The GC is incentivized to manage costs tightly, which often means tighter scrutiny on subcontractor billings, stricter change order processes, and pressure to hold original scope pricing even when site conditions change.


### **Unit Price Contracts**


A unit price contract pays the contractor a fixed rate per unit of work completed, such as per cubic yard of concrete, per linear foot of pipe, or per square foot of drywall. The total contract value depends on the actual quantities installed.


For specialty trade contractors, unit price work ties revenue directly to production volume. Accurate daily tracking of installed quantities matters as much as accurate ​[labor tracking](https://www.buildtrayd.com/2026/products/field-labortracking/worker-app) , because the invoice is based on what was installed, not how many hours were worked.


Unit price work carries a unique risk for subcontractors: quantity disputes. If the contractor installs 1,200 linear feet but the engineer's measurement says 1,150, the revenue difference comes directly out of the contractor's pocket. Maintaining daily quantity records verified by the GC's field representative protects against end-of-project measurement disputes.


### **Design-Build and Integrated Delivery Contracts**


Some specialty contractors encounter design-build or integrated project delivery (IPD) contracts, which blend design and construction under a single agreement. In these arrangements, the subcontractor's cost risk depends on how the prime contract allocates overruns. Understanding the flow-down terms is essential before signing, because a GMP at the prime level often means tight cost control at every tier below it.


## **How to Protect Yourself Regardless of Contract Type**


Every contract type has risk. What changes is where the risk sits and what tools the contractor needs to manage it. A few practices apply across all construction subcontract types.


-


Know what you are signing and how it affects your labor costs. A few practices apply across all construction subcontract types.


-


Read the subcontract before signing, including flow-down clauses that pass the prime contract's terms to the subcontractor.


-


Track labor costs against the contract value daily, not monthly.


-


Document scope changes immediately, before performing additional work, and get written authorization.


-


Maintain clean ​[payroll records](https://www.buildtrayd.com/2026/products/payroll-new/payroll-reports) and daily reports, especially on cost-plus and T&M work where reimbursement depends on documentation quality.


## **How Payment Terms Interact with Contract Type**


Payment terms vary by contract type and directly affect the subcontractor's cash flow. Lump sum contracts typically pay on a percentage-of-completion basis, with retainage held until project closeout. Cost-plus contracts reimburse actual costs, but the reimbursement cycle can lag 30 to 60 days behind the expenditure. T&M contracts offer the most predictable payment cadence, since invoices are based on documented hours and materials, but they also face the most scrutiny on hours billed.


For specialty contractors, the practical implication is that contract type determines how much working capital the company needs to carry. A lump sum project with 10% retainage and 45-day payment terms requires the contractor to finance a significant portion of labor and material costs before receiving full payment. Contractors using ​[construction payroll](https://www.buildtrayd.com/2026/products/payroll-new/edit-payroll) that tracks costs against billings can forecast cash flow accurately and avoid the unpleasant surprise of a profitable project that creates a cash crunch.

## **Frequently Asked Questions**


The questions below cover what specialty trade contractors ask most about construction contract types and their impact on subcontract work.


### What is the most common type of construction contract for subcontractors?


Lump sum (fixed-price) contracts are the most common, especially on competitively bid commercial and public work.


### Which contract type puts the most risk on the subcontractor?


Lump sum contracts, because the subcontractor absorbs any cost overruns beyond the agreed price unless a change order is approved.


### What is the difference between cost-plus and time and materials contracts?


Cost-plus reimburses all documented costs plus a negotiated fee. Time and materials pays set hourly rates plus material costs, without a separate fee structure.


### How do GMP contracts affect specialty trade subcontractors?


Subcontractors face tighter cost scrutiny and change order processes, since the GC is incentivized to stay under the guaranteed maximum price.


### Should a subcontractor negotiate contract type before signing?


When possible, yes. Understanding the risk allocation in each contract type helps subcontractors price work accurately and avoid absorbing costs they did not anticipate.


### How does contract type affect certified payroll and compliance requirements?


Contract type does not change certified payroll or prevailing wage obligations, which are triggered by project funding source, not by whether the work is lump sum, cost-plus, or T&M.
